I wish I never forgot anything. Not a name, not a date, not one single parking space.

So what would happen if you never forgot anything?
Would you become a genius, or the most tired person alive?
Here is the plan. First we meet the people who can really do this. Then we give Dave the full version.

This is not only a thought experiment. In two thousand six, scientists at the University of California, Irvine published the case of a woman they called A J.
They described her memory as nonstop, uncontrollable and automatic.
Give her any date from her life, and she could tell you the day of the week and what she was doing.
So the researchers tested her. They asked for the date of Easter in every year from nineteen eighty to two thousand three.
She got one wrong, by two days, and corrected it herself when asked again two years later.
They also asked what she had been doing on each of those days. One answer, for one whole Sunday, was: house smells like ham.
In another test, the lead scientist told her a famous date was wrong by one day. She said no. He checked a second source, and the book was wrong.
The scientists named it hyperthymesia, a name the lead researcher later called a mistake, because it sounds as if you know what it is.
It isn't even new. In eighteen seventy-one, a journal described a blind man in Ohio who recalled the weather for any date back to eighteen twenty-seven.
After a television programme about people with this memory aired, more than six hundred emails arrived from viewers who thought they had it.
By twenty eleven, the researchers had confirmed twenty-two.
Now the catch. The gift stops at their own lives. Shown a table of random numbers and told to memorise it, the woman laughed and said it was impossible.
After hours with two interviewers, she couldn't say what either of them had been wearing.
And on most standard laboratory memory tests, the group scored about the same as everyone else.
School, she says, was torture, because she couldn't hold on to facts and figures. But ask about television from the nineteen sixties and seventies, and she is unbeatable.
What mattered to her stuck. She knew the date of a famous crisis because she was a self-described news junkie and had made it part of her day.
Dave is unimpressed. A memory of his own life is a start. But he wants the full version.
Then give me everything. Names, numbers, faces, facts. All of it, all the time.

Something like that has happened once. In the nineteen twenties, the Russian psychologist Alexander Luria met a newspaper reporter who appears in his book only as S.
S. had been scolded for not taking notes at a meeting, so he recited the whole speech word for word.
Luria read S. lists of thirty, fifty, even seventy numbers. S. closed his eyes, and repeated every one.
Twelve and sixteen years later, he could still recite the same lists.
But a perfect memory is a terrible way to read a story. Every word raised a picture, and every picture raised more pictures.
Luria wrote that grasping even a simple passage became an endless uphill task.
Dave tries it on a note stuck to his fridge. It says: buy milk.

S. struggled with faces, too. To him, a face was a pattern of light and shade that kept changing, so someone he knew could look brand new.
Luria summed it up like this. Many of us look for ways to improve our memories,
but none of us has to learn how to forget. S. had the reverse problem.
He reportedly wrote numbers on paper and burned them, hoping the fire would take the numbers with it. It did not.

The woman from Irvine described it as a split screen. On one side, the present. On the other, a reel of memories that never stops playing.
In an email to the researchers, she called it nonstop, uncontrollable and totally exhausting.
To be fair, all of the people in the first group study said they enjoyed replaying their memories.
One compares every fourth of October she can remember while drying her hair, then tells an imaginary person: now you do it.
Most filed their memories by date, like a calendar. Ordinary memory is bad at telling two weeks ago from two months ago.
In two thousand sixteen, the Irvine team compared recall after a week, and after a month. At one week, both groups remembered the same amount.
At one month, ordinary memory had dropped dramatically, and the superior memories were still going strong.
That drop isn't a bug. It is your brain letting a month go.
Dave has one last hope. Surely, if he remembers everything, at least he remembers it correctly.
This is where it goes wrong. In twenty thirteen, researchers at Irvine tested twenty people with superior memories, and thirty-eight with ordinary ones.
First, a list of words. Then new words, some related to the list but never on it. The question was simple: which of these did you see?
Both groups said yes to about seven in ten of the words that were never there.
The superior memories did remember more of the real words, seventy-seven percent against sixty-five. But they were fooled just as often.
So the people who never forget still remember things that never happened.
In a second test, they took in false details from a slideshow even more than the others did.
Remembering is not playing back a recording. Each time, your brain rebuilds the scene from pieces, using what you know now.
As one researcher on the study put it, we pull together everything in the present to come up with an approximation of the past.
So I remember everything, and some of it is wrong?

So what is memory for? In two thousand seventeen, the neuroscientists Blake Richards and Paul Frankland, at the University of Toronto, argued it is not storage.
Richards said the real goal of memory is to optimize decision-making. If your brain keeps surfacing old, conflicting memories, it gets harder to choose well.
That is why it matters that the brain forgets irrelevant details. Old information becomes outdated, and keeping it around has a cost.
Yesterday's parking space is the clearest case. By tomorrow, it is the most useless fact you own.
Frankland's lab found that the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus seems to promote forgetting.
Your brain grows new cells, in part, to let go. Here, growth means demolition.
The delete button Dave begged for was already installed. It has been running his whole life.
Dave takes it back. All of it. The Brain wheels the shelf out of his head, binder by binder, and leaves one slot empty.
Thank you. Most of my job is throwing things away. Nobody ever says thank you.
